With these measures in place, the City of Inman is better protected against fraud.

Inaccurate and Untimely Return of Title IV Funds (R2T4) Planned Corrective Action: Saint Elizabeth University acknowledges this finding. The audit identified that 2 of 9 students who officially withdrew did not have Return of Title IV Funds (R2T4) calculations completed, resulting in late returns of $10,927 and $6,284 in Federal Direct Loans, and 1 student had an R2T4 prepared using an incorrect Last Date of Attendance (LDA), resulting in an additional $313 that should have been returned. Total questioned costs: $17,524. These errors were attributable to turnover in financial aid staff and the absence of a systematic withdrawal reconciliation process. The following corrective actions are being implemented in accordance with 34 CFR 668.22: Post-Semester Withdrawal Reconciliation: Following the end of each semester/payment period, the Financial Aid Office will generate a complete official withdrawal report from the student information system coordinating with the Registrar’s Office. This report will be compared against the R2T4 completion log to confirm that an R2T4 calculation has been performed for every student who officially withdrew during the period. R2T4 Timeliness Standards: SEU will adhere to the regulatory requirement that R2T4 calculations be completed no later than 30 days from the date of the institution's determination of withdrawal, and any required return of Title IV funds will be made to the Department no later than 45 days from the date of determination. Effective July 1, 2026, SEU will also implement the updated R2T4 regulations (GENERAL-26-20), including the requirement for attendance-taking institutions to document the withdrawal determination date no later than 14 days after the student's last date of attendance. Last Date of Attendance (LDA) Verification: Before finalizing any R2T4 calculation, the designated staff member will verify the LDA against all available attendance and/or activity documentation, including faculty attendance records, LMS login data, and any other institutional records. The Registrar’s Office will confirm the LDA used prior to calculation submission. R2T4 Accuracy Review: All completed R2T4 calculations will undergo a secondary review by the Director of Financial Aid or a senior FA staff member to verify accuracy prior to any return of funds to the Department. Staff Training: All financial aid staff involved in the R2T4 process will receive training on withdrawal procedures and R2T4 calculation requirements, including the updated regulations effective July 1, 2026, on an annual basis and whenever regulatory changes occur. Person Responsible: Tonya Williams, Director of Financial Aid Anticipated Completion Date: May 31, 2026 (remediation); ongoing thereafter

Need Analysis Planned Corrective Action: Saint Elizabeth University acknowledges this finding. The audit identified that 2 of 60 students were awarded subsidized Direct Loans in excess of demonstrated financial need — $5,063 and $3,011 respectively — because certain institutional scholarships were incorrectly coded in the financial aid system as excluded from Other Financial Assistance (OFA) rather than included. This caused the need calculation to be overstated, allowing subsidized loan awards that exceeded the students' actual calculated need. Total questioned costs: $8,074. The finding is classified as a Significant Deficiency under 34 CFR 685.200(a) and 34 CFR 685.102(b). The following corrective actions are being implemented: Scholarship Fund Code Audit: The Financial Aid Office will conduct a comprehensive review of all institutional scholarship and grant fund codes within the financial aid system to ensure that all institutional aid is properly flagged as Other Financial Assistance and is included in the need calculation prior to the application of the Subsidized loan. This review will be completed prior to the start of the 2026-2027 award year packaging process. Pre-Disbursement Awarding Check: A pre-disbursement review process will be implemented requiring a FA staff to confirm that all components of a student's financial aid package have been correctly categorized (OFA vs. non-OFA) and that subsidized loan awards do not exceed the student's calculated need, before disbursement is authorized. System Configuration Controls: SEU Information Technology (IT) will work with its financial aid system vendor to implement system-level controls that flag or prevent disbursement of subsidized loans when the need calculation indicates an award in excess of need, providing an additional automated safeguard. Annual Packaging Review: At the beginning of each award year, before packaging begins, the Director of Financial Aid will review and approve all fund code configurations in the financial aid system, documenting the review in writing and retaining it for audit purposes. Person Responsible: Tonya Williams, Director of Financial Aid Anticipated Completion Date: Review 2025-2026 students prior to year-end closeouts and packaging processes for the 2026-2027 award year.

Enrollment Reporting to National Student Loan Data System (NSLDS) Planned Corrective Action: Saint Elizabeth University acknowledges this finding. The audit identified that 8 of 66 students tested had enrollment statuses in NSLDS that were not reported accurately and timely, a result of SEU not completing consistent reconciliations of enrollment statuses throughout the year. All 8 students were updated during the audit process. Inaccurate or untimely NSLDS enrollment reporting can directly impact students' loan grace periods, in-school deferment eligibility, repayment start dates, and interest accrual, and constitutes noncompliance with 34 CFR 690.83(b) and 34 CFR 685.309. The following corrective actions are being implemented: Enrollment Reporting Schedule: SEU will establish and adhere to a formal enrollment reporting schedule aligned with NSLDS reporting requirements. Enrollment changes (including new enrollments, withdrawals, drops below half-time, graduations, and leaves of absence) will be submitted to NSLDS within 30 days of the roster file being sent by NSLDS, or within the timeframes required by the SAIG agreement. Roster File Reconciliation: Upon receipt of each NSLDS Roster File, staff in the Registrar's or Financial Aid Office will reconcile the enrollment statuses reported on the roster against current enrollment data in the student information system, and submit any required updates within the required reporting window. Periodic Spot Checks: In addition to responding to NSLDS Roster Files, SEU will conduct quarterly enrollment reconciliation spot checks, comparing NSLDS-reported statuses against the current enrollment records for a sample of enrolled, withdrawn, and graduated students. Results and any corrections made will be documented. Enrollment Status Triggers: SEU will establish automated or manual alert procedures for enrollment status changes that require NSLDS updates, including: semester-end enrollment confirmations, mid-semester withdrawals, grade-level changes, and program completions. Staff Training: Financial Aid and Registrar staff responsible for NSLDS reporting will receive training on the NSLDS Enrollment Reporting Guide (February 2026 version) requirements, including accurate use of enrollment status codes and reporting deadlines, on an annual basis. Person Responsible: Tonya Williams, Director of Financial Aid and Marybeth Obrycki, Registrar Anticipated Completion Date: June 30, 2026; ongoing quarterly thereafter

FISAP Reporting Planned Corrective Action: Saint Elizabeth University acknowledges this finding. The audit identified that SEU did not properly retain underlying documentation supporting the Fiscal Operations Report and Application to Participate (FISAP) submitted for award year 2023-2024, making it impossible to verify the accuracy of certain key line items. This constitutes noncompliance with 34 CFR 668.24(e), which requires institutions to maintain records supporting participation in Title IV programs for a minimum of three years following the end of the award year to which the records pertain. The following corrective actions are being implemented: FISAP Documentation Retention Procedure: SEU will implement a formal, written FISAP documentation retention procedure requiring that all data, reports, and supporting calculations used to complete each line item of the FISAP be compiled, labeled, and archived at the time of FISAP submission. Document Retention Compliance: All FISAP-related records will be retained for a minimum of three years following the end of the applicable award year (or longer if required by an ongoing audit, litigation, or other regulatory hold), in compliance with 34 CFR 668.24(e) and SEU's existing document retention policy. Post-Submission Audit File: Following FISAP submission, a complete audit file will be assembled containing the final submitted FISAP, confirmation of submission, and all supporting data. Compliance Requirement: Procurement

	Type of Finding: Compliance; Internal Control over Compliance – Significant Deficiency 
	
	Criteria or Specific Requirement: Per Uniform Guidance (2 CFR § 200.327 and 2 CFR Part 200, Appendix II), all contracts made by non-federal entities under federal awards must contain specific provisions as applicable, such as those for equal employment opportunity, Davis-Bacon, termination for cause, compliance with laws and regulations, and others. These provisions are required to ensure compliance with federal program requirements for procurement. 
	
	Condition and Context: During testing of contracts for the American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) program, we noted that contracts selected for testing did not contain all the required provisions outlined in Appendix II to 2 CFR Part 200. While services were otherwise procured appropriately, documentation of the required contract clauses was not consistent across all contracts selected for review.
	
	Cause: The City’s procurement processes did not include sufficient controls to ensure that all federally required contract provisions were incorporated into every contract funded with federal awards.
	
	Effect or Potential Effect: Lack of inclusion of all required federal contract provisions increases the risk of noncompliance with Uniform Guidance and could lead to disputes or enforcement issues if regulatory or compliance matters arise. No questioned costs were identified, as the services procured were determined to be allowable and otherwise appropriate.
	
	Recommendation: The City should enhance its procurement procedures to ensure all contracts funded by federal awards include every provision required by Appendix II to 2 CFR Part 200 as applicable. Regular review of contract templates and procurement checklists should be implemented to support compliance.
	
	View of Responsible Officials and Planned Corrective Actions: 
	
	The Purchasing Department will implement the follow items to correct deficiencies in procurements subject to federal Uniform Guidance. 
	
1.	In consultation with the Legal department, Purchasing will develop a standard contract supplement that can be attached to any City contract using federal funds. This supplement will contain clauses addressing the following: 
a.	Termination for Cause
b.	Clean Air Act
c.	Byrd Anti-lobbying Amendment
d.	Equal Employment Opportunity (for construction
e.	Federal Prevailing wages (“Davis – Bacon Act”) (for construction)
f.	Compliance with other laws and regulations as applicable
2.	During the writing of all new and recurring procurements, City departments will be asked if they anticipate using federal funds. The federal supplement will be added to the procurement checklist and will be included with IFBs/RFPs if necessary and deleted if not.

In addition, 2 CFR 200.214 requires non-Federal entities to ensure that Federal awards are not made to parties that are suspended or debarred. Finding: 2025-002 – Procurement, Suspension and Debarment - District Health Department

Auditor Description of Condition and Effect: The Department was unable to provide sufficient documentation supporting compliance with federal procurement and suspension and debarment requirements. Specifically, the Department could not provide documentation of quotes for the five vendors selected for testing. According to Department personnel, the vendors were considered sole source selections; however, the Department was unable to provide quotes or appropriate documentation to support the sole source classification. In addition, the Department did not have a formal sole source justification form at the time of the engagement. Furthermore, the Department could not provide evidence that it had verified the vendors were not suspended or debarred through any of the three allowable methods (i.e.- checking the System for Award Management (SAM) Exclusions, collecting a certification from the entity, or adding a clause or condition to the contract). Although the vendors were subsequently verified as not being suspended or debarred, documentation of the verification (including the date of the check) was not retained. Additionally, the Department did not consistently document its evaluation of whether certain agreements represented contractor or subrecipient relationships, resulting in a lack of support for the classification applied in accordance with federal requirements. The Department could not properly document compliance with federal requirements as required under Uniform Guidance. This also increases the risk that federal requirements applicable to subrecipients may not be properly applied.

Auditor Recommendation: We recommend that the Department review its policies and procedures to ensure that applicable procurement requirements are followed and documented when the Department enters into new contracts or procurement arrangements with vendors for goods and/or services of federal programs. Additionally, the Department should verify that any vendors or contractors selected are verified as neither suspended or debarred per the SAM.gov website. The Department should also ensure that it performs and documents an evaluation of each agreement to clearly distinguish between contractor and subrecipient relationships in accordance with federal requirements.

Corrective Action: Management recognizes and agrees with the recommendations of the auditors.  The County sees this as an opportunity to improve procedures and internal controls. The above questioned costs represent allowable and documented program costs and do not represent intentional errors or misstatements. Management is committed to adhering to established procedures surrounding federal and state grant awards, along with the review of applicable guidelines and procurement standards moving forward.  Additional resources will be created to ensure compliance standards are met and documented.

Responsible Person: Ben Dawson, County Administrator/Controller

Anticipated Completion Date: September 30, 2026

Finding 2025-004 – Significant Deficiency: TANF Eligibility 

1.	Condition
For 11 out of 40 taxpayer files selected for testing from a nonstatistical sample (population of 12,672 returns), there was a lack of adequate support to demonstrate that the taxpayers met all TANF eligibility criteria or clearly showed that the criteria were not met. 
2.	Cause
The Organization also receives other grants with less stringent eligibility criteria and uses similar processes to deliver services under those awards. However, the Organization does not maintain records that separately identify, track, or reproduce the populations of individuals served under each specific funding source. As a result, it was not possible to demonstrate that individuals who did not meet TANF eligibility criteria were served exclusively under other, less restrictive funding sources, and adequate records were not available to support that TANF-funded services were limited to eligible beneficiaries.
3.	Effect/Risk
Providing TANF-funded services to ineligible participants or participants whose eligibility cannot be substantiated may result in unallowable program costs being charged to the TANF grant. The noted error rate in our sample indicates there is a risk that the total population of program participants includes additional ineligible or inadequately documented beneficiaries, which could subject the client to questioned costs and potential repayment. 4.	Corrective Action Planned
Management has enhanced TANF eligibility procedures to clearly differentiate the TANF eligibility criteria from the less stringent eligibility criteria for other grants. 
5.	Responsible Party
Program Director responsible for TANF reporting, with supervisory review performed by Executive Director or Controller, as applicable.
6.	Implementation Timeline
Revised procedures and documentation requirements have been implemented for fiscal year 2026 and apply to all subsequent TANF reporting.
7.	Monitoring of Ongoing Compliance
Management reviews the TANF reporting on a quarterly basis to confirm the correct eligibility criteria has been followed.

Finding 2025-001: Over awarded Pell Grant:
Sikich tested forty files and one student received a Pell grant in excess of her allowed amount. The
student was eligible for $1233 but received 2465. The auditor recommends returning the ineligible
$1232 back to the Department of Education.
Comments on Finding and Recommendation(s): The over award resulted from a transitional
period during the implementation of Global Financial Aid Services, during which not all awards
and disbursements were processed through their system. This was a human error.
Additionally, the Student Information System (SIS) integration—used to determine enrollment
intensity and support accurate disbursements—was not fully operational. As a result, the Pell
Grant was not correctly calculated based on the students’ six (6) scheduled hours of
attendance. The institution concurs with the recommendation to return the identified over
award.
Actions Taken or Planned: The institution is now fully operational on Global Financial Aid
Services, with complete integration between the financial aid system and the SIS. This
integration ensures that awards and disbursements are accurately calculated based on
scheduled hours and enrollment intensity. All awards and disbursements are processed
through the system’s automated controls, significantly reducing the risk of manual error and
preventing recurrence of similar issues. The institution concurs with the recommendation and
will work with Global to return the $1232 of 24-25 Pell and will provide documentation to show
completion of the return.

Finding 2025-002: Under awarded Federal Direct Subsidized Loan
Sikich tested forty files, thirty of which were Federal Direct Loan recipients, and one student did not
receive the full amount of eligible Federal Direct Subsidized Loan. The auditor recommends the
Institution reallocate $180 from the students unsubsidized loan amount to the subsidized loan.
Comments on Finding and Recommendation(s): The Federal Direct Loan over award occurred
prior to the implementation of Global Financial Aid Services. At that time, proration
requirements were not correctly applied based on the defined academic year. It was a human
error made by the institution. Under current processes, this issue would have been identified
and corrected during Global’s compliance review prior to loan origination and disbursement.
The institution concurs with the recommendation to return any ineligible funds, as applicable. Actions Taken or Planned: The institution is now fully operational with Global Financial Aid
Services. Global’s compliance review processes include validation of academic year
parameters and proration requirements for Federal Direct Loans prior to origination and
disbursement. Additionally, Global staff are trained to evaluate when proration applies,
ensuring accurate loan awarding and preventing recurrence of similar findings. The institution
concurs with the recommendation and will work with Global to reallocate the $180 from
unsubsidized to subsidized. Documentation of confirmed transaction will be provided.

Finding 2025-003: Untimely Paid Credit Balance
Sikich tested forty files, thirty of which had credit balances, and one credit balance was not paid in
a timely manner. The auditor recommends the Institution increase controls over credit balances.
Comments on Finding and Recommendation(s): The student had not been attending and was
withdrawn in the 14-day period; however, the student requested to be reinstated which was
approved. This caused the delay in the payment to the student. The institution concurs that
the payment was issued outside of the 14-day window.
Actions Taken or Planned: The institution will manage credit balances to ensure that payments
are issued to students as aid is received. This finding is repeated from the prior year audit;
however, corrective action will help mitigate future instances.

Finding 2025-004: Inaccurate and Untimely Enrollment Status Reporting
Sikich tested forty files and enrollment status effective dates were either incorrectly reported or not
reported to the National Student Loan Data System (NSLDS) for two students. Furthermore, the
Institution did not provide enrollment update roster responses in a timely manner for the months of
August, October, and December in 2024 and February, April, and June in 2025. The auditor
recommends the Institution increase their controls over enrollment reporting procedures.
Comments on Finding and Recommendation(s): The institution underwent a change in their
student information system in early 2024, which created a loss in some of the automations and
integrations that existed in the old system. In July of 2024, the institution implemented services
with Global Financial Aid Services and there was a loss of access to Ed connect. The institution
concurs that controls need to be increased for enrollment reporting procedures.
Actions Taken or Planned: The institution has engaged with the National Student Clearinghouse
to finalize a master service agreement. The institution concurs with this finding and will ensure
that the enrollment response process is reviewed and completed on a monthly basis moving
forward. This finding is repeated from the prior year audit; however, corrective action will help
mitigate future instances.

Finding 2025-005: Incorrect Refund Calculation
Sikich tested fourteen drop students and found one incorrect refund calculation. The auditor
recommends the Institution refund $2464 to the Department of Education and increase controls
over refund calculations.
Comments on Finding and Recommendation(s): The incorrect refund calculation occurred
prior to the institution’s transition to Global Financial Aid Services’ Change in Status (CIS)
process. At that time, refund calculations were not subject to the automated controls and
compliance review now in place. This was a human error. Under current processes, this
discrepancy would have been identified and corrected through system reporting and review.

returned to the Department of Education.

Change in Status (CIS) process. This includes system-generated reporting and compliance
review of supporting documentation to ensure the accuracy of refund calculations. These
controls standardize the process, improve oversight, and significantly reduce the risk of similar
errors occurring in the future. The institution concurs with the recommendation and will work
with Global to return the $2464 of 24-25 Pell and will provide documentation to show
completion of the return.

Corrective actions: The Disbursement Specialist reviews the Loan Draft Requests (LDR) and verifies the expenditures to supporting documentation submitted with the requests for accuracy and allowable costs. If satisfied, the Disbursement Specialist signs and dates the LDRs indicating financial approval for payment. These are then forwarded to the engineering staff for a technical review of the LDR. The DEQ Senior Engineer or DEQ Principal Engineer performs technical reviews of the draft requests for eligibility of all costs for the Clean Water program. The Drinking Water LDRs are forwarded to the Wyoming Water Development Office to be reviewed by the DWSRF Technical Advisor. The technical reviewer signs and returns the LDR to OSLI. Upon receipt by OSLI, the Disbursement Specialist then enters the transaction into EnABLE and the WOLFS accounting system for payment, and through a two-tier approval process. EnABLE and WOLFS are not integrated.

Following the established review process of the LDRs, the Disbursement Specialist updates, prepares, and provides the following items when disbursements for first-round funds are being reviewed and approved in EnABLE and WOLFS. This is to ensure that the funds are being drawn from the correct grant and program. All payment entries in EnABLE are approved by the Senior Grants & Loans Analyst, SRF Program Financial Manager, or Assistant Director of Administrative Services Division.

• Reviewed/signed LDR;
• Loan Letter of Credit (LOC) spreadsheet filled out for reviewed LDR amount. Funding confirmed between LOC and EnABLE for WOLFS GAX document coding (each loan has its own spreadsheet detailing from which source the loan is funded);
• EnABLE loan draw request executed and print-out of pending transaction to be approved (to be signed and dated by the first approver); and
• GAX printout from WOLFS with verified budget coding in WOLFS is correct (to be signed and dated by the first approver).

A packet consisting of the EnABLE loan draw, WOLFS GAX, and the reviewed LDR are given to the Senior Grants and Loans Analyst to execute the first approval level in EnABLE and approve the GAX in WOLFS. The LDR requested amount is checked from the reviewed LDR to the EnABLE disbursement and to the GAX. The loan funding is verified and approved from EnABLE to the GAX coding. Once all items are confirmed to be correct, the Senior Grants and Loans Analyst approves the EnABLE disbursement and GAX (signs and dates the document in the packet and signs and dates the LDR process checklist).

The packet is then forwarded to the second reviewer, the SRF Program Financial Manager (or Assistant Director if not available), to duplicate the same review from the step above. If the first level of approval is confirmed, the documents are signed and dated, and the second level of approval in EnABLE is executed through the “Post Financial Activity” process. Once both levels of approval are completed, the packet is returned to the Disbursement Specialist to execute the ASAP draw.

The Disbursement Specialist assigns an LOC number, fills out the remaining section of the loan LOC spreadsheet, and confirms the Federal draw amount. The LOC sheet is printed out and placed in the disbursement packet. The Disbursement Specialist then does the following:

• Updates Sum Sheet (which corresponds to the loan LOC funding source to ensure the correct funding source). Sum Sheet is printed and placed in the disbursement packet; 
• Updates CD Sheet from which the grant funds are to be drawn from (utilizing the first-in, first-out method). The CD Sheet funding source is checked to ensure that it corresponds to the oldest available funds designated in the Sum Sheet. A copy of the CD sheet is printed and placed in the disbursement packet;
• Initiates the Federal reimbursement in ASAP. The Federal grant that matches with the CD sheet grant is chosen. If it is a DWSRF loan disbursement, the funds are pulled from the DA pot of money under the grant. If it is a CWSRF loan disbursement, the funds are pulled from the only available funding pot CA. The ASAP draw is submitted for review. On the review screen, the remaining overall grant balance is confirmed that it matches the amount on the CD sheet. If the OSLI CD sheet and ASAP system balances match, the draw is submitted with a settlement date four days out from the date of submittal (in the event that a mistake is found during the ASAP approval process, the draw can be deleted or corrected). The ASAP draw is printed out and placed in the disbursement packet;
• A CR is executed in WOLFS verifying the budget coding to the loan funding, and the CR amount is equal to the ASAP funds to be deposited from ASAP. A copy of the CR is printed out and placed in the disbursement packet; and
• The entire disbursement packet is given to the Senior Grants and Loans Analyst to be approved. The Senior Grants and Loans Analyst verifies that the amount drawn from ASAP is correct and from the correct funding pot if applicable (DWSRF only), the CD tracking sheet and ASAP balances match, and the CR line coding is correct. If everything is correct, the approver signs and dates the ASAP draw, CR, and transaction checklist.

The entire LDR disbursement packet is uploaded to the loan file in the EnABLE loan software. 

For LDRs funded from second-round funds, the process is the same, except that the items provided to the approver are limited to:
• Reviewed/signed LDR;
• Loan LOC (each loan has its own spreadsheet detailing from which source the loan is funded);
• GAX printout from WOLFS to verify the budget coding in WOLFS is correct (to be signed and dated by the approver); and
• EnABLE printout of pending transaction to be approved (to be signed by approver).

Then for both programs after the end of each month, and before new accounting transactions can be processed for the program, the programs have three balancing procedures that take place to ensure that any mistakes that may have gotten by during the approval processes are caught and corrected before proceeding. Two of them are performed by the Senior Grants & Loans Analyst and one by the SRF Program Financial Manager.

The Senior Grants & Loans Analyst performs one balancing procedure that focuses solely on the Federal disbursements and reconciles all of the revenues deposited from the ASAP draws into the 7553 Revenue Source, and the Federal amounts that are tracked to the individual loan LOC sheets. The second balancing procedure balances all of the first-round and second-round loan disbursements by comparing reports ran from the WOLFS accounting software and the EnABLE software.

Disaster Grants - Public Assistance                                                                                              FEMA Working Capital Advances (WCA)                                                                           LRA acknowledges that WCA funds received through the Puerto Rico Central Office of Recovery, Reconstruction and Resiliency (COR3), acting as the pass-through entity for FEMA Public Assistance (PA) funds, remained in the Authority’s bank account for extended periods prior to disbursement. Rather, it resulted from federal programmatic requirements that must be satisfied before FEMA-funded projects can proceed to implementation.
Several LRA projects under Disaster DR-4339 are currently undergoing FEMA review for approval of Alternate or Improved Projects, which require FEMA to complete multiple determinations before authorizing project implementation. These determinations include review and approval of the Scope of Work (SOW), Cost Eligibility (CE), and Environmental and Historic Preservation (EHP) compliance requirements, among other federal regulatory reviews. FEMA approval of these elements is a prerequisite for proceeding to final design, procurement, and construction.
The timeline for these federal reviews is outside the control of the Authority. Due to the unique environmental and historic characteristics of the former Naval Station Roosevelt Roads facilities, FEMA’s Environmental and Historic Preservation (EHP) review process has been more complex and time-consuming than originally anticipated. Until FEMA completes these required reviews and issues the necessary approvals, LRA cannot initiate project activities that would generate eligible expenditures; therefore, invoices cannot be incurred or paid using the advance funds during this period.

COVID-19 - Coronavirus State and Local Fiscal Recovery Funds (SLFRF)               Noncompliant with Procurement Procedures
We strongly object to the findings. This finding is grounded on an incomplete interpretation of the applicable framework, as the funds in question were properly classified as Government Services pursuant to Resolution 2024-05 issued by AAFAF. In that regard, the Resolution expressly recognizes that: “Based upon the information currently provided, LRA's proposal is likely eligible as Government Services, which generally include any service traditionally provided by a government...” This classification is determinative, as it defines the nature of the funds and the applicable compliance structure.
Furthermore, the Resolution itself establishes the operational and collaborative framework under which the project was executed, confirming that the initiative is not a traditional procurement scenario but a coordinated governmental effort. Specifically, it provides that: “To achieve this goal, LRA and the Municipality of Ceiba will be providing assistance, collaboration, and support for the redevelopment process.” Therefore, the structure of the project aligns with an intergovernmental collaboration model, consistent with the Government Services designation, and does not support the finding of noncompliance under a standard procurement analysis.
Consistent with this framework, it is important to clarify that the collaborative agreements referenced in the audit correspond to prior arrangements funded with Federal awards, including those under ALN 21.027 Coronavirus State and Local Fiscal Recovery Funds, under which the Authority retained responsibility for compliance with applicable Federal requirements during their term. However, such collaborative agreements have since concluded and are no longer in effect. Accordingly, any past, current, or ongoing activities are governed by applicable state laws and regulations, as contemplated under the applicable federal framework and the Government Services classification.
Moreover, the applicable federal regulatory framework expressly contemplates and permits the use of state procurement and administrative procedures in the execution of federally funded activities. In this context, the Authority implemented and managed the collaborative arrangements in accordance with the applicable state legal framework, treating such arrangements as intergovernmental agreements rather than traditional  procurement contracts. This approach is fully consistent with the nature of the Government Services classification and the collaborative structure endorsed by AAFAF.
Management further represents that, during the term of such agreements, it maintained appropriate oversight over activities performed pursuant to these collaborative arrangements with the Municipality of Ceiba, and that such activities were carried out in good faith and in substantial compliance with the requirements applicable at that time. This further confirms that the audit finding, which appears to rely on a procurement-based analysis, does not accurately reflect the legal and operational framework governing these activities.
In addition, we included and provided supporting documentation evidencing compliance with the requirements applicable to this funding. Such documentation was submitted as part of the administrative record and demonstrates adherence to the governing framework, further reinforcing that the activities conducted were consistent with the applicable legal and regulatory provisions. The below includes the recommendation and our corrective action plans for the 2025 Audit Findings. Finding 2024-003 and 2025-001 - Reporting We recommend the University review its internal control procedures and implement additional review procedures to ensure data is accurately reported to the NSLDS and within the required timeframes. Regardless of whether a student record error was either (a) made by Saint Louis University (SLU) itself or (b) “created” by the NSC due to its own limitations as described in Response #1 above, those errors need to be corrected. When, for whatever reason, the NSC identifies SLU graduation data as erroneous, Office of the University Registrar (OUR) can identify such student records via an error reporting process provided by the NSC. The NSC requires SLU (and all institutions) to correct any such erroneous records within 30 days. There are three issues to address as OUR evaluates why SLU has failed to always rectify errors within that 30-day window. First, that 30-day window is not, in fact, always a 30-day window. Some student records, at some point during the 30-day window, are locked by the NSC when the NSC receives enrollment data updates about those students; the NSC’s system cannot both (a) process new enrollment records for a student while (b) SLU also attempts to correct errors related to graduation status. So, for students whose enrollment records change during that 30-day period, SLU is locked out of the NSC’s system to correct graduation status errors. If, therefore, for example, a student’s erroneous graduation records have been “open” for SLU remediation for 10 days but then the NSC locks the records because that student also has updated enrollment records in process, SLU’s window for correcting the erroneous graduation records has been limited to just 10 days. If the NSC re-opens that record before the full 30-day window has expired, NSC will re-open the graduation record for SLU to re-attempt correction. However, that again requires regular SLU monitoring of the changing file statuses and a window for correction less than the prescribed 30 days. The amount of manual monitoring of this system for record compliance and remediation is extensive, and particularly problematic given the staffing limitations of the OUR. The second issue impacting SLU’s ability to remedy erroneous responses within the 30-day window is that the NSC’s systems cannot “handle” multiple graduation-related changes when students are/have been enrolled in more than one SLU program at a time. In other words: SLU sometimes cannot – due to NSC data system limitations – make the necessary corrections to graduation data for a student’s first program (“Program A”) when the student is also still enrolled in a second program (“Program B”). In fact, if SLU changed graduation data for Program A, it would result in new errors related to the student’s accurate, continuous enrollment (pre-graduation) in Program B. SLU cannot “win” either way in this predicament; one way or another, SLU’s records in the NSC will be “wrong” (depending on your vantage point).
One remedy to this situation is for the OUR to regularly inform the Office of Student Financial Services (SFS) of the situation and request SFS manually update the records directly in the NSLDS system (to which the OUR does not have access). The OUR will implement this change to controls going forward, knowing that this represents additional manual monitoring and action. The third issue to address is similar. Due to flaws in the NSLDS’ own systems, the NSLDS does not record the accurate graduation dates for a select set of students (those whose graduation dates are different from their last dates of enrollment at SLU). In these cases (as in the situation above), the OUR cannot remediate this via its access to the NSC; the problem must be resolved in the NSLDS system, to which the OUR Registrar does not have access. Accordingly, the remedy to this situation is for the OUR to regularly inform the (SFS) of the situation and request SFS manually update the records directly in the NSLDS. The OUR will implement this change to internal controls going forward, knowing that this represents additional manual monitoring and action. Alex DeLonis, Assistant Vice President for Student Financial Services, is responsible for addressing the above item by May 2025.

Corrective Action(s): During COVID-19, HPD adopted HUD CARES Act waivers that temporarily suspended adverse actions to protect applicants, participants, owners, and staff. While recertifications were still requested from February 2020 through December 2021, families were not penalized for incomplete submissions, resulting in a backlog. HPD has since implemented technological and process improvements to address this backlog, increasing its HUD reporting rate, with further improvement expected in FY2026. Although COVID-era policies have ended and normal enforcement processes have resumed, HPD continues intensive follow-up efforts to ensure compliance, and full recovery to pre-pandemic certification levels will take additional time.

1. Continue to build on existing systems to more closely track recertifications that are mailed and not returned. 
a. Although the number of cases without a recertification completed was greater in this year’s single audit sample than last years, this is not reflective of the actual trend in the agency’s overall number of completed recertifications, which increased significantly in calendar year 2025.  Between 06/30/2024 and 06/30/2025, HPD’s recertification rate increased by 10 percentage points. We expect the percentage of completed recertifications to increase in the upcoming year. This reflects the steady effort required to both reduce a backlog of cases and prevent additional cases from becoming overdue. HPD continues to employ successful strategies that have resulted in this progress to further reduce overdue recertifications in the coming year.  
b. A technical update is scheduled for the spring of 2026 which will automate the upload of submitted recertification packages into HPD’s digital case files, which will improve the efficiency for follow-up on both returned and unreturned recertification packages. 

2. Implement revised HPD policy to allow updates to Utility Allowances during all certifications including those processed for rent increases and interim changes. 

3. Continue to use Community Based Organizations (CBOs) for referring overdue cases in order to assist participants in completing and returning recertification packages. 
a. HPD continues to use contracted CBOs to assist participants in meeting program requirements. CBOs are located in three of the five boroughs with the most participants. Referrals are primarily for seniors and people with disabilities who need help completing and submitting their recertification packages to HPD on time. HPD has transitioned from individualized referrals to a systematized approach to identify and refer households for quicker action by CBOs.  A daily report of referred cases is sent to the team coordinating and prioritizing CBO referrals.

4. Continue to provide automated reminders for participants at risk of termination of assistance because of their failure to submit a recertification package. 

5. Continue to differentiate roles among teams to streamline efficient completion of annual Recertifications. 

6. Continue to meet the training needs of new and existing staff members to empower more staff members in the processing of annual certifications to minimize delays in processing of annual certifications. 

Anticipated Completion Date: June 2026

The delays to properly updating and reporting changes in student enrollment statuses to NSLDS were due to deficient internal administrative controls over the enrollment reporting process as the financial aid department went through changes in personnel and updates to the communications module. The result of these actions had identified that there were inconsistent reporting, procedures, and staff training was confirmed as necessary and needed. It was determined that the responsibilities for reporting enrollment changes to NSLDS and the steps necessary were not clearly defined, resulting in missed deadlines.
The implementation of the following to correct the timely enrollment reporting:
•	The College’s President engaged a higher education specialist through their relation with the law firm Rouse, Frets, White, Goss, Gentile, Rhodes, P.C. to work with the College administrative staff to complete a review of the mandatory financial aid compliances, and provide guidance to the final aid staff to ensure that the College is satisfying the necessary requirements and proved oversight and consult during the review of policies and procedures to ensure completion and submissions of the documentation are stratified. 
•	Our Institutional Research staff are sending out attendance summary records for financial aid and the Registrar to review during the census determination period and at the semester midpoint. The students who are identified as being absent or missing from their coursework are contacted by administrative staff and the College’s Care Team to discuss any circumstances that have caused them to miss classes or to counsel them if they were planning on withdrawing from the College. The new Financial Aid team has partnered with the staff from Student Life, the Success Coaches, and the athletic staff to help monitor any unofficial withdrawal students.
•	Students identified as being absent without reason are monitored by the team identified about and communication is provided to the Financial Aid Director who now is monitoring these students to ensure that completion of the required documents and updates to student status reports are completed and that the reporting in NSLDS is finalized within 60 days of any withdrawal.
•	Additionally, training was provided to the Financial Aid Director and staff as to the procedures that are required when reviewing any student who had completed a semester with reported grades of all Fs to ensure that enrollment status is reported correctly.
•	The College has relocated both the Registrar’s office and the Financial Aid office to be in the same building so that communications can be easily done daily between the teams to ensure proper monitoring of student status and enrollment updates are completed.

Corrective action: Management acknowledges this repeat finding regarding enrollment reporting noncompliance. The University is strengthening policies and procedures by developing comprehensive written procedures for NSLDS enrollment reporting, including specific protocols for handling fatal error fields and implementing escalation procedures when NSLDS discrepancies are identified.

The University will provide comprehensive training to Financial Aid and Registrar staff on enhanced data validation protocols and new error monitoring systems, cross-train backup personnel to ensure continuity during absences or staff transitions, establishing automated calendar reminders for monthly reporting deadlines, and establish regular management review of NSLDS compliance metrics and internal audit testing of reporting accuracy and timeliness.

The review identified deficiencies in procurement practices, specifically related to (1) the use and
documentation of appropriate procurement methods in accordance with 2 CFR §200.320, and (2) the lack
of documented standards addressing conflicts of interest as required under 2 CFR §200.318(c).

The organization will revise and strengthen its written procurement policies and procedures to
ensure full compliance with federal requirements. This includes:
o Clearly defining procurement methods (micro-purchases, small purchases, sealed bids,
competitive proposals, and noncompetitive procurements).
o Establishing thresholds aligned with current federal regulations.
o Requiring adequate documentation to support the method of procurement selected.
o Implementing standardized procurement checklists to ensure consistency and compliance.
2. Conflict of Interest Policy Implementation (2 CFR §200.318(c)):
The organization will develop and formally adopt a written conflict of interest policy that:
o Prohibits employees, officers, agents, and board members from participating in
procurement actions where a real or apparent conflict exists.
o Requires annual disclosures of financial and personal interests.
o Establishes procedures for identifying, documenting, and mitigating conflicts.
3. Training and Capacity Building:
All staff involved in procurement and financial management will receive mandatory training on
federal procurement standards, including 2 CFR Part 200 requirements. Training will be conducted
annually and upon onboarding of relevant personnel.
4. Internal Controls and Oversight:
o A supervisory review process will be implemented to ensure procurement transactions are
properly documented and compliant prior to approval.
o Periodic internal audits will be conducted to monitor adherence to updated policies.
5. Documentation and Recordkeeping:
The organization will maintain complete and accurate procurement records, including rationale for
procurement method, contractor selection, price analysis, and conflict of interest disclosures.
We are in the process of implementing the forementioned corrective actions, with implementation no later
than the end of the June 30, 2026 fiscal year end.
The organization is committed to strengthening its internal controls and ensuring full compliance with
federal procurement standards moving forward.

Views of Responsible Officials: We concur with the finding. IDOE had no formal monitoring framework to evaluate LEA compliance with SNS. Description of Corrective Action Plan: IDOE will take the following corrective actions to fully address each deficiency noted:

1.	Develop and Implement a Written SNS Monitoring Procedure
●	IDOE’s Monitoring and Compliance Director will create a comprehensive, written SNS Monitoring Procedure outlining:
o	The SNS requirement and expectations for LEA compliance;
o	Required documentation LEAs must submit;
o	The steps IDOE will use to review compliance;
o	Roles and responsibilities for IDOE staff; and
o	Required timelines for review and follow-up.
●	This written procedure will align with IDOE’s responsibility to maintain effective internal controls under 2 CFR 200.303 and will reference internal control expectations included in FMC 4.1 Section 5(b)(2).
●	By April 30, this written procedure will be reviewed annually.

2.	Publish Guidance for LEAs
●	IDOE’s Monitoring and Compliance Director will prepare and disseminate SNS Guidance for LEAs that provides:
o	A clear explanation of the SNS requirement;
o	Required documentation;
o	LEA responsibilities; and
o	Examples of allowable and unallowable scenarios.
●	This guidance ensures LEAs understand federal expectations and reflects the finding’s recommendation for clear communication with subrecipients.
●	Guidance will be provided to LEAs through a Learning Lab Session and will be posted in our weekly updates to LEAs and through Moodle.
●	By May 31, LEA guidance will be reviewed annually.

3.	Create Monitoring Tools and Review Criteria
●	IDOE’s Monitoring and Compliance Director will develop tools to support consistent evaluation of LEAs, including:
o	An SNS review checklist;
 

o	A documentation review template;
o	Criteria for making determinations;
o	A standardized SNS determination form to document conclusions.
●	These tools will ensure staff apply SNS requirements consistently and that determinations are well-documented. This aligns with the monitoring expectations in 2 CFR 200.332(e)
(pass-through entity monitoring).
●	By July 31, these tools will be reviewed annually.

4.	Staff Training on SNS Requirements and Processes

FINDING 2025-008


Finding Subject: Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIP) - Special Tests and Provisions – Medical Loss Ratio (MLR) 

Contact Person Responsible for Corrective Action: Kathleen Leonard
Contact Phone Number and Email Address: 317.233.9282; Kathleen.Leonard@fssa.in.gov

Views of Responsible Officials: 

FSSA disagrees with the findings for the audit as data used to calculate annual Medical Loss Ratios is thoroughly reviewed by OMPP and our external actuary. The audit finding indicates that the current process is deficient because the MLR data is compared with an MCE audited financial report that is not GAAP Medicaid specific.

FSSA believes that the annual audited financial reports collected from the health plans do meet federal requirements. 

FSSA/SBOA is awaiting feedback from CMS regarding the MCE submissions for the specific Medicaid program. We sent follow up to CMS to determine the outcome of their review. 

Explanation and Reasons for Disagreement: 

OMPP has a very robust collection process for items used in the MLR calculations. Because a risk corridor was implemented for all managed care programs beginning in 2020, there have been no MLR recoupments for years 2020 through 2023 as the risk corridor recoupments result in MLRs at or above required levels.

OMPP has been working with both our external actuaries as well as the Managed Care Entities (MCEs) to collect financial data necessary for the oversight of our managed care programs. MCEs did submit audited financial results for 2025 that included allocations to show specific results for Indiana Managed Care programs. 

FSSA is relying on guidance from a CMS FAQ document that indicates that the requirement that audits “be conducted in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles and generally accepted auditing standards” does not designate a specific accounting method that must be used. CMS indicated that GAAP, Statutory or GAS accounting methods would be considered acceptable. 

Description of Corrective Action Plan: 

FSSA has shared this CMS FAQ from 2017 with the audit team which lays out the guidance and requirements for these audits.  The audit team indicated that templates that are used to submit information to CMS indicate that GAAP audits are required.  The audit team indicated that templates that are used to submit information to CMS indicate that GAAP audits are required. 

CMS has confirmed that GAAP audited financial reports are not required. Instead, the state may accept financial reports prepared under Statutory Accounting Principles (SAP) that MCEs submit to IDOI. However, because SBOA does not believe the SAP reports meet Medicaid-specific requirements, they have submitted the MCE SAP reports along with the Medicaid-specific appendices to CMS for review to determine whether they satisfy the Medicaid Specific requirements.
 
Until CMS responds that the Medicaid specific appendices meet this requirement, the SBOA finding will remain unchanged.  If we do not wait for CMS’s response, the alternative solution would be to require MCEs to submit Medicaid-specific GAAP or SAP reports. The MCEs have indicated that this would be costly and burdensome.

Anticipated Completion Date: 

FSSA/SBOA is awaiting CMS feedback on how to move forward. This matter is expected to be finalized by May 2026. The MCEs will be notified whether the financial reports submitted for 2025 continue to meet the State’s requirements, and a determination on the type of audit report required for 2026 will be made by the end of June 2026 if not.

If specific Medicaid-only SAP or GAAP reports are determined to be required, OMPP/SBOA will coordinate with the MCEs to establish a realistic preparation timeline and set an appropriate deadline for completion and will require our new actuarial vendor to review them as required for the MLR.

Views of Responsible Officials:

Description of Corrective Action Plan:

Annual SF-425 Financial Reports (FFRs)

The FFY23 report for Grant 2302INSOSR was submitted by DCS, but it was determined after the submission of the FFR the drawdown was made from an incorrect grant. To correct this, DCS staff contacted the federal agency to process a JV correction. As a result, the total federal agency has denied the FFR that was submitted.

DCS’ Division Director of Finance has been working with the federal agency to resolve the issue. Since this is the Final FFR, the amounts are prefilled in PMS. PMS will need to update the information in their system before DCS can resubmit the report.

Once the PMS system is updated, our Budget Analyst will review the report. Following the review and approval by the Division Director, the Budget Analyst will resubmit the corrected report.

Going forward, DCS will perform the following actions to ensure accurate reporting in PeopleSoft Financials, the federal payment system, and the Annual SF-425 Financial Reports (FFRs):
 
1.	DCS Finance staff working with federal grants will be required to review, and acknowledge the review, of the FMC 4.1 guidance on federal grants.
2.	As part of its monthly reconciliation process, DCS Finance staff will continuously track reimbursements as compared to PeopleSoft records when funds are drawn from the federal payment management system (PMS).
3.	Prior to submitting the annual financial report, the Budget Analyst will ensure amounts in PeopleSoft reconcile to those in the payment management system (PMS).
4.	The Division Director will perform a secondary review of the reconciliation performed by the Budget Analyst prior to finalizing and certifying the FFR report.
5.	DCS’ Division Director will modify the existing standard operating procedure (SOP) to reflect this process.


Post-Expenditure Report


The Post Expenditure Report was submitted by previous DCS staff, and it was reported inaccurately. Since the report had already been certified by the federal agency, current staff believed the submission was correct. We have contacted our federal representative for guidance and will follow their direction once next steps are provided.

The Budget Analyst will prepare the corrected report, which will be reviewed and approved by Director Federal Fiscal Oversight and Risk.

Going forward we have added additional approval steps increasing the level of approval to the Director of Federal Fiscal Oversight and Risk. This ensures we have a proper level of oversight and internal controls. This also ensures that even with staffing changes the approval process will continue through upper-level management. DCS will ensure accurate reporting by performing the following steps:
1.	DCS Budget Analyst will send the template for the post-expenditure report to each grantee agency sixty (60 days) prior to the due date of the Federal Report in March.
2.	As post-expenditure reports are received, the Budget Analyst will run a PeopleSoft query, SOIPC009D, to ensure the total expenditure amount matches what was submitted by the grantee agency.
3.	The grantee agency submission will then be combined into a consolidated post-expenditure report by the Budget Analyst. This consolidated report reflects the information that must be entered into the SSBG Collection Site and corresponds to OMB Control Number: 0970-0234. All reports are stored on the DCS Finance Shared Drive for recordkeeping purposes.
 
4.	The consolidated post-expenditure report is reviewed by the Budget Analyst and Division Director prior to being sent to the Director Federal Fiscal Oversight and Risk for final review and approval.
5.	Once approval is received, the information from the consolidated post-expenditure report is manually entered into the SSBG Portal by either the Budget Analyst or the Division Director for submission to the Office of Community Services, within the Administration for Children & Families.



Federal Funding Accountability and Transparency Act (FFATA)


For future FFATA reporting, DCS will be creating a standard operating procedure (SOP) to address this finding and ensure accurate and timely federal reporting. The SOP will contain the following elements:
1.	A reconciliation between the amounts in the SAM.gov system and the subawards made from the federal grants will be conducted prior to starting the FFATA. This reconciliation will be completed by the Budget Analyst and reviewed by the Division Director.
2.	Any backlog entries not reported in the preceding fiscal year or FFATA will be entered into the report. These backlog entries will be reviewed by the Budget Analyst and approved by the Division Director.
3.	The identification of any PeopleSoft reports and other reporting tools that will be used to identify grantees that have met the threshold for reporting. These will be reviewed annually for any necessary reporting tool updates.
4.	Prior to the submission of the FFATA, a secondary level of review will be provided by the Director Federal Fiscal Oversight and Risk to ensure proper internal controls.
5.	Annual training will be provided to all DCS Finance staff that will participate in federal reporting activities.
6.	DCS will review the SOP annually to ensure it is aligned with federal requirements.
7.	In addition, DCS Finance will recommend that our Internal Audit team include the FFATA in their annual audit plan for review and validation.



Anticipated Completion Date:
DCS has started to work with our federal partner on making the necessary corrections. DCS is hopeful that corrections and enhanced internal controls can be implemented by June 30, 2026.

5.	Policy and Procedure Updates:

In connection with this review, the University identified invoiced amounts associated with incorrectly classified budget categories and has refunded $243,852.41 to the Pennsylvania Department of Health (PADOH) in full.

To address the identified control deficiencies and prevent recurrence, the University has implemented and continues to formalize enhanced controls over the grant invoicing process. (1) reconcile invoice line items to the underlying general ledger detail, and
(2) compare year-to-date expenditures to the approved award budget by category to ensure allowability, accuracy, and compliance with budget constraints.

Additionally, all invoices are digitally signed by the reviewing post-award grant analyst prior to submission, providing evidence of review and creating an auditable record of approval.

The University is further strengthening preventive and detective controls by developing a formal grant invoicing policy and enhancing monitoring processes. The formal policy will codify roles and responsibilities for invoice preparation, review, approval, and submission; require documented budget-to-actual monitoring; and require that any reallocation of costs between approved budget categories be supported by sponsor approval, preferably through a formal budget amendment, prior to invoice submission.

In addition, the University is implementing an enhanced invoice-tracking and monitoring process within the post-award office to ensure that all expected invoices are prepared, reviewed, and submitted through the appropriate control structure. This process will include identifying and investigating exceptions, such as instances where invoicing activity does not align with expected billing patterns, to support the timely detection and resolution of discrepancies.

Finding 2025 001
Prior-Year Coronavirus State and Local Fiscal Recovery Funds Expenditures Included in the Current-Year SEFA
Corrective Action Plan
The Organization records expenses in QuickBooks using the accrual basis of accounting, with each transaction coded to its specific grant using grant/customer level designation. At the time an expense is incurred, management records accruals directly to the appropriate expense account and assigns the applicable grant class, ensuring that costs are attributed to the correct funding source.
To strengthen year end accuracy and prevent prior period costs from being reported in the incorrect SEFA period, management will implement a formal year end SEFA cutoff and reconciliation process. This process will include:
•	Reviewing all grant related expenses recorded near year end to confirm they were incurred within the correct fiscal year.
•	Recording accrual journal entries by grant in QuickBooks for costs incurred but not yet invoiced at June 30.
•	Reconciling accrued expenses to supporting documentation, including payroll reports, vendor statements, contracts, and service period confirmations.
•	Reconciling total grant expenditures per the general ledger (by grant class) to amounts reported on the SEFA.
Because all accruals are tagged with the appropriate grant/customer in QuickBooks, this process ensures that federal expenditures are reported in the correct audit period and by individual grant, in compliance with Uniform Guidance requirements.

Finding 2025 002
Current-Year Coronavirus State and Local Fiscal Recovery Funds Expenditures Recorded in the Subsequent-Year SEFA
Corrective Action Plan
Management will continue to record grant expenditures based on when costs are incurred, not when invoices are received, using accrual accounting within QuickBooks. All accrual entries are already booked by grant, using the Organization’s grant specific class structure, which allows expenditures to be tracked and reported accurately on a per grant basis.
To address this finding, management will enhance consistency and oversight by implementing the following controls:
•	A standardized year end grant accrual checklist identifying all grants with activity near fiscal year end.
•	A required reconciliation of accrued expenses by grant class to ensure that all current year costs are reflected in the appropriate SEFA period.
•	Verification that subsequent year invoices tied to prior year services are matched to existing accruals rather than recorded as current year expenses.
•	Review and approval of the final SEFA by the Controller, with documentation supporting the timing and allocation of expenses.
These procedures, combined with the existing grant level coding in QuickBooks, ensure that expenditures are properly classified by grant and by fiscal year, allowing the Organization to meet federal reporting requirements and avoid misstated SEFA amounts in future periods.

Corrective Action Plan
Management will implement a documented review and approval system for all nonfinancial reports submitted to granting agencies, including programmatic and performance reports.
The new process will include the following components:

o	This cross check ensures consistency between financial activity and reported program outcomes.

Criteria or Specific Requirement (Including Statutory, Regulatory, or Other Citation):

Pursuant to November 2025 Compliance supplement, Eligibility: 

The HOME program has income targeting requirements. Only low-income or very low-income persons, as defined in 24 CFR section 92.2, can receive housing assistance (24 CFR section 92.1). Therefore, the participating jurisdictions must determine if each family is income eligible by determining the family’s annual income, including all persons in the household, as provided for in 24 CFR section 92.203. The participating jurisdictions must maintain records for each family assisted (24 CFR section 92.508). 
Pursuant to 24 CFR section 92.216, Income targeting: Tenant-based rental assistance and rental units: 
Each participating jurisdiction must invest HOME funds made available during a fiscal year so that, with respect to tenant-based rental assistance and rental units: 
(a) Not less than 90 percent of: 
(1) The families receiving such rental assistance are families whose annual incomes do not exceed 60 percent of the median family income for the area, as determined and made available by HUD with adjustments for smaller and larger families (except that HUD may establish income ceilings higher or lower than 60 percent of the median for the area on the basis of HUD's findings that such variations are necessary because of prevailing levels of construction cost or fair market rent, or unusually high or low family income) at the time of occupancy or at the time funds are invested, whichever is later; or 
(2) The housing units assisted with such funds are occupied by families having such incomes; and 
(b) The remainder of: 
(1) The families receiving such rental assistance are households that qualify as low-income families (other than families described in paragraph (a)(1) of this section) at the time of occupancy or at the time funds are invested, whichever is later; or 
(2) The housing units assisted with such funds are occupied by such households.

Cause:
The policies and procedures for the City's HOME funded Tenant Based Rental Assistance program were not very specific related to contractor requirements for file documentation maintenance regarding client income changes and corresponding rent subsidy changes.

Effect:
The City could potentially be out of compliance and provide incorrect subsidy to participants or provide subsidy to ineligible participants.

Questioned Costs:
None.

Context:
See condition above for the context of the finding.

Recommendation:
We recommend the City enhance its internal controls by updating its Tenant Based Rental Assistance program guidelines to provide specificity related to contractor requirements for file documentation maintenance regarding client income changes and corresponding rent subsidy changes.

The Department will formally reissue the Records Management Process and Protocol and require all units to adhere to standardized procedures for document storage, including the use of designated network drives and approved file structures.

·         Assignment of Accountability at the Unit Level
Unit leadership will designate responsible personnel to oversee compliance with records management requirements, ensuring that critical documentation is properly maintained and accessible.
 
·         Standardization of File Organization and Naming Conventions
The Department will reinforce standardized naming conventions, file structures, and access protocols to ensure consistency and ease of retrieval across all program areas.
 
·         Ongoing Compliance Monitoring
The Department will implement periodic compliance checks to ensure adherence to records management requirements and to identify and remediate any gaps in documentation practices.
 
·         Training and Communication
The Department will conduct targeted training and communication efforts to ensure that all staff understand documentation expectations, proper storage procedures, and the importance of maintaining audit-ready records.
Through these actions, the Department is strengthening enforcement of its existing records management framework to ensure that documentation supporting compliance with federal program requirements is consistently maintained, centrally accessible, and readily available for audit.

However, MDH respectfully disagrees with the finding insofar as it indicates that potentially ineligible persons were served by the program.
MDH asserts that all 12 individuals identified were eligible for services under 42 USC 300ff-26(b). While the administrative status field was marked "Unknown" for reasons detailed below, the client records contained verified viral load and CD4 count data with associated dates.
●	Per COMAR 10.18.05.02. D. Medical Criteria. To meet the medical criteria the individual shall be infected with HIV as verified by the Department.
●	The Department meets this verification requirement through data matching with our state HIV registry which includes the most recent confirmed laboratory results. 
●	MDH performs monthly surveillance data matches and reviews to update this clinical data in our MADAP client data system. At no point was any individual in the reports found to lack the clinical data that supports an HIV diagnosis as reviewed, investigated, and accepted for inclusion in the state HIV registry. Consequently, there is no evidence that benefits were provided to "ineligible claimants."
The finding attributes the issue to a "system update." MDH clarifies that the "Unknown" status is a historic data convention used when a specific AIDS-defining stage was not explicitly documented in the original record, despite a confirmed HIV diagnosis. This was communicated to the auditor during discovery.
Recognizing the potential for ambiguity, MDH proactively identified these legacy markers in 2024 (prior to the audit) and updated the Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs). The updated SOP requires Eligibility Specialists to manually transition these records to "HIV-Positive/AIDS Unknown" which is now necessitated as the HIV field moves away from AIDS as a diagnostic marker. This was communicated to the auditor during discovery. However, as a non-clinical reviewer, the auditor did not request a copy of MADAP SOPs to understand the process for determining eligibility. 
Corrective Action Plan
●	MDH will continue the systematic update of the status field as clients who initially presented for program participation when AIDS was a defining category during recertification and renewal. 
●	MDH will remove the “Unknown/unreported” option in the Patient’s HIV status box.
●	Moving forward, MDH will ensure that HIV positive status is clearly reflected in the primary field to avoid administrative ambiguity, while continuing our monthly surveillance data matches and reviews as a secondary internal control.

Finding 2025-002- U.S. Department of Education (ED) Student Financial Assistance
Programs - Failure to Reconcile Title IV Programs (Material Weakness)
Condition: The University did not perform required reconciliations between the Office of
Financial Aid and the Business Office for the following Title IV programs during the audit period:
• Federal Pell Grant Program
• Federal Direct Student Loans
• Federal Supplemental Educational Opportunity Grant (FSEOG)
• Federal Work-Study (FWS) Program
As a result, disbursement records maintained by the Office of Financial Aid did not reconcile to
the general ledger or COD for any of the programs reviewed. No documentation of monthly or
year-end reconciliations was provided for audit examination.
Corrective Action: The condition resulted from the absence of formalized procedures,
inconsistent process execution, and personnel turnover, which affected continuity, standardization,
and oversight.
Allen University has implemented formal reconciliation processes that include biweekly and
monthly reviews, standardized checklists, and enhanced oversight controls to ensure accuracy,
consistency, and timely completion.
